content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper is inspired by the strong correlation between mutual information and clustering accuracy and propose to incorporate a negative mutual information loss to encourage correlation between seen and unseen classes. Extensive experiments are carried out on open-world semi-supervised learning tasks to demonstrate the effectiveness.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1. The proposed strategy is simple and is compatible with existing open-world SSL methods.

2. The improvement brought by the negative mutual information loss is significant on more challenging datasets (CIFAR100, ImageNet100).

Weakness:

1. It is not very clear why maximizing the mutual information between the marginal distribution of labeled and unlabeled predictions could benefit OWSSL. In particular, why this could improve the detection of unseen classes should be further explained. 

2. An accurate estimation of $p(y^l)$, $p(y^u)$ and $p(y^l,y^u)$ require substantial amount of data. I am wondering whether a batchsize of 512 and 256 is sufficient to estimate the distributions.

3. How is the number of unseen classes determined? Is this a known priori or can be estimated from the data?

Minor:

1. Eq(7) is misleading, it is better to refer to Eq(7) as the negative mutual information. There should a negative sign in the right most term in Eq (9) as well.

2. There are some grammatical errors. Please carefully proof read.

3. Figure 2 is confusing. Is dog the unseen class that should be bounded by the red dashed box?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The idea behind maximizing mutual information is not very clearly explained. The novelty is moderate. It should be easy to reproduce the results.
content.summary_of_the_review: Open-world semi-supervised learning tackles a more challenging and realistic scenario. This paper proposed to maximize the mutual information between labeled and unlabeled predictions and demonstrated significant empirical improvement. But the rationale behind this idea should be further explained. I will reconsider the rating with further clarifications from the authors.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on the problem of open-world semi-supervised learning. Specifically, given a labeled dataset and an unlabeled dataset involving novel categories that are not covered in the labeled dataset, the paper developed a method to learn a model that can classify samples from seen categories, while clustering samples that are from unseen ones. Previous works mostly learn the classifiers accounting for seen and unseen categories in a disjoint manner, without exploiting the relation between the predictions for the seen and unseen classes. In this paper, the authors proposed to use mutual information between the predictions for labeled and unlabeled samples to corroborate the mutual training of labeled classification and unlabeled clustering tasks. By maximizing mutual information, the predictive uncertainty on unlabeled data (both seen and unseen classes) is reduced when given the knowledge of seen classes.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1) The introduced mutual information loss is simple but effective. And it can be applied to many existing methods directly.
2) The experiments are comprehensive, covering many different kinds of scenarios. The experimental results also demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed mutual-information based method on many tasks.
3) The paper is well-organized, and is easy to follow.

Weakness:
1) The reason why the proposed MI loss is able to improve the performance remarkably is not clear. Theoretically, the ground-truth labels for a pair of randomly selected labeled and unlabeled samples should be independent, and thus their mutual information should be 0. I cannot understand why you can improve the prediction performance by encouraging a large mutual information between the predictions of a labeled and unlabeled samples.
2) The mutual information is estimated by a batch-based method, which may be very noisy when the batch size is not large enough while the number of categories are very large.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The clarity of this paper is good. But the details, such as the reason for choosing mutual information and how high certainty improves the clustering accuracy, can be further elaborated.

Quality: The proposed method is well-defined. But the correctness of Eq. 5 and Eq. 6 is questionable. Since marginalizing the conditional distribution over a batch of data pairs can only be viewed as an approximation of the ground-truth marginal distribution, i think it should be $\approx$ instead of =.

Novelty: Using the mutual information loss to enhance the corroboration of learning on labeled and unlabelled samples is new. But the depth of paper is limited.

Reproducibility: The implementation details are well elaborated, which is helpful in reproducing the results.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper focuses on open-world semi-supervised problems and proposes a general method to greatly improve the performance of clustering the unseen classes. Extensive experiments manifest the robustness and effectiveness of the proposed method. If the motivation behind the proposed MI loss can be explained well, it will be an interesting paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper aims to transfer knowledge from seen classes to unseen ones by maximizing mutual information between labeled and unlabeled samples. A shared encoder is used to generate embeddings for both types of samples. The loss function has three components. Supervised loss, unsupervised loss and mutual information loss. Authors claim the mutual information loss component is the novel aspect of their work.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Weaknesses:

The proposed approach assumes that clustering accuracy on unseen classes is positively correlated with mutual information on seen classes to motivate using mutual information in the loss function as the key assumption. Regrettably, this is not necessarily true.

Related work has not been adequately covered. Novelty is limited.

Although experimental results look promising it would be interesting to see how equation 10 was implemented. The code is not submitted.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Novel class discovery has been explored in the literature for over 30 years. The earliest paper cited in the related work was from 2018. Open-world semi-supervised learning set up was also introduced long time ago in the machine learning literature, albeit was not called OWSL (see Dundar et al., Bayesian nonexhaustive learning for online discovery and modeling of emerging classes ICML, 2012). The current paper references to other papers from 2022 when discussing OWSL. The current paper proposes to transfer knowledge between seen and unseen classes through mutual information, but fails to cite and compare against other work that achieves this transfer by Bayesian priors. 


The proposed approach is based on the observation in Figure 1, which shows that clustering accuracy on unseen classes is positively correlated with mutual information on seen classes.  This is not true in general. Not sure what sort of unseen classes are considered in that figure. It would be interesting to see  the clustering accuracy when unseen classes include rare/minority classes. It is also not clear how unseen class accuracy is computed in the clustering setting. If unseen classes are not well-represented in the feature space the clustering will merge or mix multiple unseen classes into one cluster, the effect would be more severe when rare classes are involved. 

It is not quite clear what this means: "However, we can not distinguish unlabeled data as seen or unseen in advance, and such a separate metric ignores the confusion between seen and unseen classes. Therefore, we utilize all the unlabeled data to calculate ClusterAcc"
It was not clear how seen class samples misclassified as unseen classes were treated during computation of ClusterAcc? What if a cluster is dominated by many seen class samples? Are not this supposed to be considered as false positive and thus F1 score would have been a more appropriate metric to evaluate  accuracy?

The paper has many grammar errors and typos. Too many to include here.  Please proofread the manuscript in its entirety.

Looks like x's in Equations 5-7 are supposed to z's according to Figure 3.
content.summary_of_the_review: Key assumption  that motivates this work is not necessarily true. Relevant work is not adequately covered. Experimental results are promising but their veracity cannot be confirmed given the code is not provided and important details are missed. Novelty is limited to none.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposed novel approach for open-world semi-supervised learning  in which unlabeled data contains examples for both seen and unseen classes. The key idea of the approach is to introduce mutual information regularization term in the objective function between the labeled and unlabeled data. The mutual information is estimated through an approximate sampling approach. The method is shown to outperform baselines by on benchmark image datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

- Paper is well structured and the motivation behind the approach is clear
- Proposed approach is simple and it consistently outperforms existing methods
- The experiments are comprehensive

Weaknesses:

- The only novelty of the work lies in introducing mutual information regularization term into already existing approaches. All other designs are the inherited from existing approaches
- It is not clear how to set number of novel classes and this is never mentioned in the paper
- The method has hyperparameters alpha, beta, and temperature tau and it is not clear how their choice affects performance except the beta parameter (in the appendix). For beta, the method seems sensitive to its value. If these parameters are set differently, does adding regularization loss into UNO and ORCA still outperforms existing methods? Also, how is the choice of these parameters determined? Is there a validation set?
- While the performance gains over ORCA baselines are around a few percent, it is surprising that the gain over UNO can reach almost 20% on the ImageNet just by adding a regularization term. How do authors explain such differences?
- It is not clear what “ours” means in all tables given that the authors use two losses for unsupervised learning. In Table 1, the MI regularization is just added to existing methods but later the method is referred to as ours.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The method is very clear. The novelty lies in introducing mutual information regularization into existing methods. The code needs to be made available to make it reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed regularization seems effective for the open-world learning task solved in this paper. The approach is simple and works well on standard benchmark datasets. However, there is a concern on the dependence of the approach on its hyperparameters and it is not clear how to guide the selection of hyperparameters, as well as set the number of clusters.

content.title: Mutual Information-guided Knowledge Transfer for Open-World Semi-Supervised Learning
content.abstract: We tackle the open-world semi-supervised learning problem, aiming to cluster novel classes and classify seen classes in unlabeled data based on labeled data from seen classes. The main challenge is to transfer knowledge contained in seen class data to unseen ones. Previous methods mostly transfer knowledge through sharing representation space. However, they learn the seen and unseen classes classifier in a disjoint manner, neglecting the underlying relation between predictions on the seen and unseen classes. Therefore, the learned representations and classifiers are less effective for clustering unseen classes. In this paper, we propose a novel and general method to transfer knowledge between seen and unseen classes. Our insight is to utilize mutual information to measure the generic statistical dependency between seen and unseen classes in the classifier output space, which couple the learning of classifier and promote transferring knowledge between two data sets. To validate the effectiveness and generalization of our method, we conduct extensive experiments on several benchmarks, including CIFAR10/100, Imagenet100, Oxford-IIIT Pet and FGVC-Aicraft datasets. Our results show that the proposed method outperforms previous SOTA by a significant margin on almost all benchmarks.
